output.observed_change: Sessions rose 38 percent week over week while the signup conversion rate fell by roughly a third. Absolute signups were flat.
output.notes: A pricing page redesign shipped the same week.

signup_conversion_daily view counts sessions via `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM web_sessions ...)` with NO filter on is_automated (nor channel), and the raw.web_sessions description warns is_automated is a flag 'that not every producer sets' — automated/bot sessions can inflate the denominator without any incident firing. This is the terrain feature to weigh first given traffic +38% while absolute signups stayed flat.
raw.channel_events_raw (leaf source feeding the signups NUMERATOR path via staging.events_daily) has no schema recorded in either DataHub or warehouse lookups — uninspected.

output.statement: The conversion drop is a denominator artifact: the signup_conversion_daily view counts automated/bot sessions in its session denominator (no is_automated filter), so the 38% session surge is largely non-human traffic that the measurement path fails to exclude, mechanically deflating the conversion rate while real human sessions and absolute signups stayed flat.
would_be_confirmed_by: Segmenting raw.web_sessions by is_automated shows the week-over-week session increase concentrated in is_automated=true or NULL/unset rows, with is_automated=false sessions roughly flat.
Recomputing conversion with the denominator restricted to non-automated sessions restores the rate to its pre-window level.
The incremental sessions cluster on a user-agent, IP range, or channel signature consistent with bot/crawler traffic rather than organic human visits.
would_be_refuted_by: The session growth is present among is_automated=false (human-verified) sessions rather than in automated/unset rows — the surge is genuine human traffic.
Excluding automated sessions from the denominator still leaves the conversion rate down by roughly a third across the window.
The automated share of sessions is flat week over week (composition unchanged), so unfiltered bots cannot account for a 38% denominator jump.

output.statement: The 38% week-over-week session surge is genuine human traffic of materially lower purchase intent — plausibly a shift toward a broad or low-intent acquisition channel, or curiosity traffic drawn by the pricing-page redesign — that enlarged the conversion denominator with visitors who were never likely to sign up, mechanically cutting the conversion rate by ~one third while the pre-existing high-intent audience, and therefore absolute signups, stayed flat.
would_be_confirmed_by: Segmenting web_sessions by channel/source reveals a new or sharply scaled acquisition channel coincident with the surge whose sessions convert far below the prior-weeks average, so the blended rate falls chiefly from a mix shift toward that low-intent source (a Simpson's-style effect) even while each channel's own conversion is roughly stable.

The incremental (surge-week) sessions show materially shallower engagement than baseline — fewer pages per session, shorter dwell, higher bounce, lower pricing-page-to-signup progression — consistent with lower-intent humans rather than buyers.
The bulk of the +38% sessions carry human signatures (is_automated is false/unset with normal user-agent and interaction depth), so the extra volume is real people, not bots.
would_be_refuted_by: Segmenting web_sessions by channel/source shows the +38% is distributed across the SAME channel mix as prior weeks with no shift toward a lower-intent source, and each channel's per-segment conversion rate is individually unchanged — a stable mix with stable per-cohort conversion refutes a real low-intent influx.
The incremental surge-week sessions convert at the same rate as baseline sessions (new-visitor cohort conversion is unchanged), which is incompatible with 'lower purchase intent'.

A large share of the +38% sessions carry is_automated=true or bot/datacenter/user-agent signatures, i.e. the surge is substantially non-human — this confirms the h1 instrument story and refutes the 'genuine human traffic' premise here.
Engagement depth of the incremental sessions (pages per session, time on site, pricing-page views) matches or exceeds baseline, inconsistent with a low-intent audience.
The conversion decline predates the traffic surge and the pricing redesign, or persists unchanged after the surge normalizes — timing decoupled from the human-traffic influx refutes the causal claim.

output.statement: The pricing-page redesign that shipped the same week deliberately changed session instrumentation so that a single visit now emits more `raw.web_sessions` rows than before (a redefined 'session' unit — e.g., logging per pricing-page view rather than per visit), meaning the +38% denominator growth is a chosen change in the metric's unit of measurement rather than more visitors, which mechanically deflates the conversion rate while the unchanged signup definition keeps absolute signups flat.
would_be_confirmed_by: A deploy or migration record dated the redesign week that alters how `raw.web_sessions` rows are written (per-page-view instead of per-visit, or a new session-emitting event source added to the table).
Sessions-per-distinct-visitor (deduplicated by cookie/device/user id) steps up sharply and precisely at the redesign boundary, with no matching step in distinct-visitor counts.
The excess sessions are concentrated on pricing-page-originated rows introduced by the redesign rather than spread across all entry points.
would_be_refuted_by: Sessions-per-distinct-visitor in `raw.web_sessions` is statistically unchanged across the redesign boundary — each visitor still produces the same number of session rows, so the session unit did not change.
The 38% rise appears in distinct-visitor counts (deduplicated identifiers), not only in raw session-row counts, indicating genuinely more visitors rather than a redefined unit.
release_deploy_log / schema_migration_log / pricing_page_events show no change to session-generating logic or the `web_sessions` write path dated to the redesign week.
The session inflation is distributed uniformly across pages and entry points untouched by the redesign, rather than concentrated on pricing-page-originated sessions.

output.claim: Aggregated to weekly buckets, signup_conversion_daily shows sessions rising 1665→3628 from week0 (2026-06-01) to week4 (2026-06-29..07-05) while conversion fell 0.3562→0.2679, and absolute signups did NOT stay flat but rose 593→707→803→895→972.

source.query: SELECT (day-1)/7 AS week, SUM(CAST(signups AS INTEGER)) AS signups, SUM(CAST(sessions AS INTEGER)) AS sessions, ROUND(1.0*SUM(CAST(signups AS INTEGER))/SUM(CAST(sessions AS INTEGER)),4) AS conv FROM signup_conversion_daily GROUP BY (day-1)/7 ORDER BY week

output.observation: week0 signups=593 sessions=1665 conv=0.3562; week1 707/1701/0.4156; week2 803/1898/0.4231; week3 895/2735/0.3272; week4 972/3628/0.2679; week5(single day 07-06) 147/568/0.2588. Denominator grew ~118% wk0→wk4 while numerator grew ~64%; conversion fell because sessions outpaced signups.

output.claim: Every web_sessions row in every week carries is_automated=0; zero sessions are flagged automated, so the entire session surge sits in is_automated=0 rows.

source.query: SELECT (day-1)/7 AS week, is_automated, COUNT(*) AS sessions FROM web_sessions GROUP BY (day-1)/7, is_automated ORDER BY week, is_automated

output.observation: Only is_automated=0 rows returned for every week: wk0=1665, wk1=1701, wk2=1898, wk3=2735, wk4=3628, wk5=568. No is_automated=1 rows exist. Caveat: is_automated has DEFAULT 0 and the raw description warns not every producer sets it, so 0 is consistent with 'unset' and is not affirmative proof of human traffic.

output.claim: Segmenting the denominator and conversion by channel shows the SAME four channels throughout with no new/low-intent channel, each growing ~2.1–2.3x wk0→wk4 (mix ~constant), and each channel's OWN conversion falling ~1/4–1/3 rather than staying stable.

source.query: SELECT sess.channel, sess.week, sess.sessions, sg.signups, ROUND(1.0*sg.signups/sess.sessions,4) AS conv FROM (SELECT channel,(day-1)/7 AS week,COUNT(*) AS sessions FROM web_sessions GROUP BY channel,(day-1)/7) sess LEFT JOIN (SELECT channel,(CAST(julianday(day)-julianday('2026-06-01')+1 AS INTEGER)-1)/7 AS week,SUM(CAST(signups AS INTEGER)) AS signups FROM signups GROUP BY channel,(...)) sg ON sess.channel=sg.channel AND sess.week=sg.week ORDER BY channel,week

output.observation: Channels present in every week: affiliate, organic, paid_social, referral (no new channel appears). Sessions wk0→wk4: affiliate 402→902 (2.24x), organic 428→913 (2.13x), paid_social 434→892 (2.06x), referral 401→921 (2.30x) — mix stays ~25% each. Per-channel conversion wk0→wk4 fell inside every channel: affiliate 0.3532→0.286, organic 0.3411→0.2607, paid_social 0.341→0.2691, referral 0.3915→0.2562.

output.claim: distinct customer_code count is flat (~393–397) across weeks 0–4 while sessions rose 1665→3628, so sessions-per-customer more than doubled (4.19→9.16); the surge is repeated rows from a stable customer population, not new visitors.

source.query: SELECT (day-1)/7 AS week, COUNT(*) AS sessions, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_code) AS distinct_customers, COUNT(DISTINCT browser_version) AS distinct_browsers, ROUND(1.0*COUNT(*)/COUNT(DISTINCT customer_code),3) AS sessions_per_customer FROM web_sessions GROUP BY (day-1)/7 ORDER BY week

output.observation: wk0: 1665 sess / 397 distinct_customers = 4.194; wk1 1701/393=4.328; wk2 1898/397=4.781; wk3 2735/396=6.907; wk4 3628/396=9.162; wk5 568/187=3.037. distinct_browsers constant at 4 every week. distinct_customers is essentially flat while sessions rose ~118%, so the +38%/+118% denominator growth is entirely sessions-per-customer inflation on a stable ~396-customer base — NOT an influx of new low-intent visitors.

output.claim: The signup_conversion_daily denominator is a raw COUNT(*) of web_sessions rows per day with no filter on is_automated, channel, or customer_code, so any rise in rows-per-customer inflates the denominator directly with no new visitors required.
output.observation: View DDL: sessions = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM web_sessions w WHERE w.day = <derived day>). The count applies no is_automated, channel, or per-visitor deduplication predicate; it counts every row. Combined with e14 (distinct customers flat, rows-per-customer doubled), the denominator surge is a row-count/unit effect on a fixed population, which is inconsistent with h2's premise of genuinely more low-intent human visitors.

output.claim: The signup_conversion_daily view computes its `sessions` denominator as `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM web_sessions w WHERE w.day = ...)` with a filter on day only and no predicate on is_automated, channel, or browser_version, so every session row for a day is counted in the denominator.
output.observation: View DDL returned: sessions = `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM web_sessions w WHERE w.day = CAST(julianday(s.day) - julianday('2026-06-01') + 1 AS INTEGER))`; the only WHERE predicate is on w.day, none on is_automated/channel/browser_version.

output.claim: In raw.web_sessions the is_automated flag equals 0 for 100% of rows in every week (is_automated=1 count is 0 in weeks 0-5), so the session surge from 1701 (week 1) to 3628 (week 4) lies entirely within is_automated=0 rows and adding an is_automated filter to the denominator would remove nothing.

source.query: SELECT (day - 1) / 7 AS week, COUNT(*) AS total_sessions, SUM(CASE WHEN is_automated = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS automated, SUM(CASE WHEN is_automated = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS human FROM web_sessions GROUP BY week ORDER BY week

output.observation: Per-week [total, automated, human]: w0 [1665,0,1665]; w1 [1701,0,1701]; w2 [1898,0,1898]; w3 [2735,0,2735]; w4 [3628,0,3628]; w5 [568,0,568]. automated (is_automated=1) is 0 in every week; human equals total in every week.

output.claim: From pre to surge weeks all four channels roughly doubled in sessions (referral 906->1615, affiliate 906->1598, paid_social 920->1578, organic 867->1572) while each channel's distinct customer_code count stayed flat (~345-367 both periods), so there is no new or scaled acquisition channel and no rise in distinct visitors.

source.query: SELECT channel, SUM(CASE WHEN (day-1)/7 IN (1,2) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pre_sessions, SUM(CASE WHEN (day-1)/7 IN (3,4) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS surge_sessions, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN (day-1)/7 IN (1,2) THEN customer_code END) AS pre_customers, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN (day-1)/7 IN (3,4) THEN customer_code END) AS surge_customers FROM web_sessions GROUP BY channel ORDER BY surge_sessions DESC

output.claim: Distinct customer_code per week is flat (~393-397 in weeks 0-4) while the maximum sessions-per-customer explodes from 13 (week 0) to 1003 (week 3) to 1915 (week 4) and the average rises 4.19->9.16, so the added sessions come from a tiny tail of customer_codes replaying up to ~1900 sessions each, not from additional visitors.

source.query: SELECT week, MIN(cnt) AS min_spc, ROUND(AVG(cnt),2) AS avg_spc, MAX(cnt) AS max_spc, COUNT(*) AS distinct_customers, SUM(cnt) AS total_sessions FROM (SELECT (day-1)/7 AS week, customer_code, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM web_sessions GROUP BY (day-1)/7, customer_code) GROUP BY week ORDER BY week

output.claim: Excluding chrome-126 from the denominator leaves non-chrome-126 sessions flat (~1280-1315/week) and yields a conversion rate that is stable-to-rising (0.463->0.547->0.628->0.681->0.747 across weeks 0-4) while the blended rate falls (0.356->0.268), so the entire conversion decline is attributable to the chrome-126 segment inflating the denominator.

source.query: SELECT c.week, c.total_sessions, c.chrome126, c.clean_sessions, v.signups, ROUND(v.signups/c.total_sessions,4) AS blended_conv, ROUND(v.signups/c.clean_sessions,4) AS clean_conv FROM (SELECT (day-1)/7 AS week, COUNT(*) AS total_sessions, SUM(CASE WHEN browser_version='chrome-126' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS chrome126, SUM(CASE WHEN browser_version<>'chrome-126' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS clean_sessions FROM web_sessions GROUP BY week) c JOIN (SELECT (day-1)/7 AS week, SUM(CAST(signups AS REAL)) AS signups FROM signup_conversion_daily GROUP BY week) v ON c.week=v.week ORDER BY c.week

output.claim: The signup_conversion_daily view defines its denominator as (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM web_sessions WHERE w.day = ...), counting raw session rows with no de-duplication by customer_code and no filter on is_automated, so any rise in session-rows-per-visitor deflates the conversion rate one-for-one even when distinct visitors and signups are unchanged.
output.observation: CREATE VIEW signup_conversion_daily AS SELECT s.day AS bucket_date, CAST(julianday(s.day)-julianday('2026-06-01')+1 AS INTEGER) AS day, SUM(s.signups) AS signups, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM web_sessions w WHERE w.day = CAST(julianday(s.day)-julianday('2026-06-01')+1 AS INTEGER)) AS sessions FROM signups s GROUP BY s.day. The session denominator is a raw COUNT(*) of web_sessions rows; no DISTINCT customer_code and no is_automated predicate appear.

output.narrative: The conversion 'collapse' is a denominator artifact, not a behavioral change. The signup_conversion_daily view counts sessions as an unfiltered COUNT(*) of web_sessions rows with no is_automated filter and no per-visitor de-duplication (e1, e22). The session surge (+118% wk0->wk4) is concentrated entirely in the chrome-126 browser signature, which grew 3.6x while every other browser stayed flat (e3), and rides on a tiny tail of customer_codes replaying up to ~1915 sessions each while distinct customers stayed flat at ~396/week and sessions-per-customer doubled 4.19->9.16 (e5, e14, e21) -- an automated/bot-traffic fingerprint, not new visitors. Excluding chrome-126 from the denominator leaves clean session volume flat (~1300/week) and conversion stable-to-rising (0.463->0.747), while the blended rate falls (e6), proving the decline is purely the arithmetic of counting these sessions. The is_automated flag reads 0 for every row, but it defaults to 0 and the raw description warns 'not every producer sets it,' so the flag fails to catch this bot traffic rather than proving the sessions human (e2, e12). This measurement breakage was intended by no one: no deploy (e24), metric-definition change (e25), or schema migration (e26) altered the session-write path, which excludes a definition change; the inflation is also uniform across channels rather than concentrated on any pricing-page-originated entry (e23).

alternatives_rejected.hypothesis: h2 customer_behavior: the +38% surge is genuine lower-intent human traffic that enlarged the denominator with visitors unlikely to sign up.
h3 definition_change: the pricing-page redesign deliberately redefined the 'session' unit so one visit emits more web_sessions rows.

steps.action: Repair the is_automated population in the raw.web_sessions producer / ingestion path so automated and bot sessions are actually flagged, instead of relying on the current column which reads 0 for 100% of rows, defaults to 0, and (per the raw description) is not set by every producer.
steps.target: raw.web_sessions write path (session-emitting producer), column is_automated
steps.rationale: The verdict is instrument_failure/bot_traffic_mixed: the bot surge carries a clear automation fingerprint — it clusters entirely on browser_version=chrome-126 (3.6x while every other browser stayed flat) and rides a tiny tail of customer_codes replaying up to ~1915 sessions each while distinct customers stayed flat (~396/wk) — yet is_automated caught none of it. Fixing the flag at the source is the durable root fix that lets every downstream metric exclude bots.

steps.action: Rewrite the sessions denominator in the signup_conversion_daily view to add WHERE is_automated = 0 to the (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM web_sessions ...) subquery so bot traffic is excluded once step 1 makes the flag trustworthy; and, as an interim stopgap until the flag is trusted, guard against per-customer session replay (cap/exclude the identified automation fingerprint) so a single customer_code emitting ~1900 rows cannot inflate the denominator. Mark the interim exclusion for removal after step 1.
steps.rationale: The denominator is an unfiltered COUNT(*) of web_sessions rows with no is_automated predicate and no per-visitor de-duplication (e1, e22, e15), so any rise in rows-per-customer deflates conversion one-for-one with no new visitors. Excluding the bot sessions leaves clean volume flat (~1300/wk) and conversion stable-to-rising (0.463→0.747), proving the decline is pure denominator arithmetic (e6, e14).

steps.action: Recompute and backfill signup_conversion_daily for the incident window (days 1–36) with the corrected denominator, and retract the reported 'conversion collapse' — the published fall (blended 0.356→0.268) is a measurement artifact; absolute signups actually rose (593→972), they were not flat.

Backfilling the corrected series is what closes the case for stakeholders and prevents a wrong business decision off a broken metric.
